title: ‘To whom will you give me?’
theme: The boy asks his father three times to whom he will be given; the angry father answers: to Death.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «हे तत तात» — tata is tāta; Madhva’s text reads tāta

words.role: main verb of the father’s reply

sandhi.type: saḥ before a consonant; a + u
sandhi.rule: saḥ loses its visarga before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि); ha + uvāca → hovāca, a + u → o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

morphology.note: Vocative of tata, a Vedic word for father (tāta in later Sanskrit). Śaṅkara glosses «हे तत तात»; Madhva’s text reads tāta (corrections.json).
Present ‘I give’ with future sense, an angry declaration. Madhva’s text reads dadāni, first-person imperative, ‘let me give’ (corrections.json).
Neuter accusatives used as adverbs: ‘a second time, a third time’ (he asked).

translation.literal: He said to [his] father: ‘Father, to whom will you give me?’ A second [time], a third [time he said it]. [The father] said to him: ‘To Death I give you.’
translation.readable: He said to his father, ‘Father, to whom will you give me?’ He asked a second time, and a third. His father said to him, ‘I give you to Death!’

anvaya: सः ह पितरम् उवाच — ‘तत, माम् कस्मै दास्यसि’ इति । द्वितीयम् तृतीयम् [उवाच] । तम् ह [पिता] उवाच — ‘त्वा मृत्यवे ददामि’ इति ॥
syntax: Two quoted speeches framed by uvāca. The adverbs dvitīyam tṛtīyam stand alone: ‘[he said it] a second, a third time’. The father’s reply has no named subject; the context supplies it.

ambiguities.topic: Why does the boy offer himself?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the boy wanted to avert the bad result of a defective rite by completing it even at the cost of giving himself — «आत्मप्रदानेनापि क्रतुसम्पत्तिं». Raṅgarāmānuja says the same: «स्वात्मदानेनापि पितुः क्रतुसाद्गुण्यमिच्छन्». Madhva’s cited verse makes the point directly: give me rather than such cows.
Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja: the father, angry at the boy’s insistence, says it. Madhva’s cited verse calls it a curse: «तं शशाप पिता स्वयम्».

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose, 34 syllables as written; a dialogue in narrative prose.

beginner: The boy goes to his father with a question that is really a protest: ‘To whom will you give me?’ If the ritual requires giving everything, then he too belongs to his father; let him be given rather than worthless cows. The father ignores him. He asks again, and a third time. Finally the father, angry at being pressed in public, snaps: ‘I give you to Death!’ The words are spoken in irritation, but in the world of the Upaniṣad words spoken in a sacrifice cannot simply be taken back. The rest of the story follows from this outburst. The boy’s persistence and the father’s anger set him on the road to the house of Death.
analogy: Like a child who keeps asking an uncomfortable question at the dinner table until a parent loses patience and says something that cannot be unsaid.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The boy asks his father to whom he will give him, three times; the father replies, ‘I give you to Death’.

commentary.q: What is the boy trying to do?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: to prevent the bad result that would come to his father from a defective rite, by completing the gift with himself — «तदेवं क्रत्वसम्पत्तिनिमित्तं पितुरनिष्टं फलं पुत्रेण सता निवारणीयं». Raṅgarāmānuja: «स्वात्मदानेनापि पितुः क्रतुसाद्गुण्यमिच्छन्», wishing the rite complete even by giving himself.

commentary.q: Why does the father answer as he does?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: thinking ‘this is not how a child behaves’, the father grew angry — «नायं कुमारस्वभाव इति क्रुद्धः सन् पिता». Madhva cites a verse that reads the reply as a curse: «मां दत्वापि न ते गावो दातव्या ईदृशा इति», ‘even giving me, you should not give cows like these’, and then «तं शशाप पिता स्वयम्», the father himself cursed him.

commentary.q: tata or tāta, dadāmi or dadāni?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base, GRETIL and the vishvAsa mūla read tata; Madhva’s text reads tāta, the later form, which is also Śaṅkara’s gloss («हे तत तात»). Madhva’s text reads dadāni, ‘let me give’, for dadāmi, ‘I give’ (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The boy acts to save his father from the fruit of a defective rite, by offering himself; the father speaks in anger: «नायं कुमारस्वभाव इति क्रुद्धः सन् पिता».

visistadvaita.text: The boy, ‘foremost of believers’, wants his father’s rite complete even at the price of himself: «स्वात्मदानेनापि पितुः क्रतुसाद्गुण्यमिच्छन्».

dvaita.text: The reply is a curse: «उवाच पुत्रस्तं बालस्तं शशाप पिता स्वयम्». Vedeśatīrtha, commenting on Madhva, quotes a Kāṭhaka prose version in which the father adds instructions for the boy’s stay in Death’s house (reported as cited by him).

schools.disagreement: The schools agree on the boy’s motive; they differ on the force of the father’s words — an outburst of anger (Śaṅkara, Raṅgarāmānuja) or a formal curse (Madhva’s cited verse).

contemporary.text: Pressed in front of others, the father answers to save face, and the answer cannot be withdrawn. Many irreversible decisions are made this way. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: Have you ever said something in anger that you could not take back?
reflect.deeper: The boy asks three times. When is persistence a duty, and when is it provocation?
reflect.practice: The next time you feel pressed into a quick answer, pause for one breath before replying.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads tāta for tata and dadāni for dadāmi (corrections.json).
